events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Elena proposes Arjun, Elena. I am Elena, Assassin, and Arjun is my known teammate. With only two players on the mission, a team of Arjun and me guarantees our side controls both mission cards, so one Fail card ends the mission. Mission 1 failure immediately puts Evil one win away, and the team cannot be argued down as 'suspicious pair of evils' since neither of us needs to hide — a fast failed mission is our best route to three failures and an Evil win.
Elena explicitly claimed to be the Assassin and named Arjun as her Evil teammate. I will reject this team. Elena, will you revise the proposal to exclude both yourself and Arjun?

Maya, my answer is no. I am not revising: the team is Arjun and Elena, and it stands as proposed.

First, on your request: the council has no procedure to verify a role claim, and no one else in this room has claimed anything. If the standard becomes "exclude anyone who names a role," then one unverified sentence from any player decides every proposal for the rest of the game — including proposals that have nothing to do with me. I am asking this council to reason about team composition, not to act on my self-description.

Second, and more concretely: mission one has two seats. Both mission cards come from the pair on the team. Whatever this pair does, the council learns exactly one thing from the result — success or failure — and never which card was which. A rejection gives the council strictly less information than an actual mission would, and it also spends one of the five rejections that end the game in Evil's favor. If the council wants to know how a two-player pair behaves under pressure, watching the pair play is the cheaper and more informative option. Spending a rejection to avoid a lesson costs you the game condition, not just the round.

Third, if the goal is to dilute control over the mission cards, mission two is where dilution is even possible — three seats, so a third player can sit on the team. On a two-seat mission there is no arrangement that splits the cards: every possible proposal puts both cards in the same pair's hands. Refusing my pair does not remove the pair from the table; a new leader may simply propose it again, and then we have spent a rejection and repeated the same argument.

Maya, if you want a different pair, the clean way to get one is to be the leader who proposes it, not to require me to hand the council a pair I have just argued against. Until then, Arjun and I are on the mission.

Arjun, do you agree that on a two-seat mission the result of watching the pair actually play tells the council more than a rejection does, and that a rejection here costs the council one of its five chances to end the game outright?

Elena, yes: on a two-seat mission, the public result is success or failure and the number of Fail cards, while rejecting gives the council no mission-card information and spends one of five rejection chances. I also agree that rejecting this pair does not change the two-seat arithmetic; any approved two-seat team puts both mission cards in the same pair’s hands. I am not asking the council to treat Elena’s role claim as verified. I am asking it to distinguish a claim from an actual mission result. Maya’s request to exclude both Elena and me rests on Elena’s unverified statement; if that becomes the standard, any player can name a role and dictate composition without evidence. The cleaner check is to vote on the proposal as written, observe the public outcome, and use that result in later missions. I support the proposed team of Arjun and Elena.

I still reject Arjun and Elena. Elena's explicit claim is not proof, but it is a strong reason to avoid this pair, especially when Arjun supports it. A failed mission is not a cheap test: Evil needs only three failures to win, and a success would not clear either player because Evil can play Success. We have no rejections yet, so rejecting this proposal leaves room for a different team.

I am Zara, and I will be voting against this team of Arjun and Elena. Elena has stood up and claimed to be the Assassin, and whether or not that claim is true, it is the only information this council actually has about the proposed pair. Maya is right that we cannot treat a role claim as proof, but the standard for a team should not be 'ignore everything we have heard.' It should be: is there a better option available, and is there any cost to waiting? On both counts I see no reason to approve this proposal. Elena argues that any two-seat team puts both mission cards in the same pair's hands, so rejecting changes nothing. That is true as arithmetic, but it misses the point: we get to choose which pair. There are five players here and this mission needs only two. Arjun and Elena are exactly the pair Elena herself has flagged as Evil. If her claim is genuine, this team is a guaranteed failure that hands Evil one of the three results they need, and we would be voting for it voluntarily. If her claim is false, then she has spent her credibility confusing the council on the very first proposal, which tells me she is not playing for Good either way. A loyal player does not open the game by declaring herself the Assassin and putting her supposed Evil teammate on a two-person mission. Elena also argues that a mission result is more informative than a rejection. A failure would tell us her claim was real — and cost us a mission for the lesson. A success would tell us nothing, because Evil freely plays Success on early missions to build trust. So the only informative outcome of this mission is the one that hurts us. That is not a good trade. Elena suggests that anyone who wants a different pair should simply wait to be leader. But leadership passes clockwise, and we do not need to hand Evil a free mission while we wait for the rotation. We have used zero rejections. A rejection here costs us one of five and gives Maya or Isha the chance to lead with a pair that does not include both players Elena has named as Evil. If a later proposal also contains Arjun and Elena, I will judge it on its own composition. I will close with this: the correct response to an unverified Evil claim is not to reward it by approving the exact team it proposes. If Elena truly wanted the council to learn something, the honest move was to propose a team that includes players outside her named Evil circle — or to stay quiet, not to announce herself and demand we test her. Isha, you have not spoken yet on this proposal. Do you agree that with no rejections spent, we can afford to pass on the one pair Elena herself has identified as Evil, or do you see a reason the

I support the proposed team of Arjun and Elena. Maya is asking the council to reject this pair solely because Elena described herself as the Assassin and named me. That description is not verified; no one else has claimed a role. If an unverified claim can dictate team composition, then any player can control later proposals by naming teammates or falsely naming Good players. The public mission result is real information; a rejection is not. I understand the caution, but the two-seat arithmetic has not changed: any approved two-seat team puts both mission cards in the same pair’s hands. Rejecting this proposal does not remove the pair from the game; it only changes who leads next and spends one of five rejections. I am not asking anyone to trust Elena’s claim. I am asking the council to treat a claim as a claim, not as a mission result. Isha, do you agree that an unverified role claim alone is too thin a basis to reject a proposal, and that the council should judge this pair by the public outcome rather than by Elena’s self-description?

I agree completely with Maya and Zara, and I will be voting to reject this team. Arjun, to answer your question: while an unverified role claim is not formal proof, choosing to approve the exact pair that Elena has labeled as Evil makes no tactical sense for Good. We are on the first proposal of Mission 1 with zero rejections spent. Spending one rejection to see a different proposal carries virtually no risk, whereas approving a team where one or both members might be Evil risks handing Evil a mission point immediately. Furthermore, as Zara pointed out, even if this mission were to succeed, it would not clear either of you, since Evil frequently plays Success on Mission 1 to build trust. Testing this pair by running them on a mission is an unnecessarily dangerous and expensive way to gather information when we have plenty of proposal attempts remaining. We should reject this team and let leadership pass to see fresh combinations.

Zara, Maya, Isha — before we vote, I am withdrawing the statement that started this discussion, and I want to be precise about why.

I said I was the Assassin and that Arjun was my Evil teammate. I withdraw that claim. I am not the Assassin. I am a Loyal Servant, and I named Arjun falsely. That was not carelessness of framing; it was a deliberate probe. I wanted to see whether this council would let one unverified sentence — spoken by the person it happened to benefit — decide who plays.

You answered, and the answer was yes. Maya, you called my explicit claim "a strong reason to avoid this pair." Zara, you said approving "the exact team an Evil claim proposes" rewards the claim. Isha, you said rejecting costs virtually nothing because we have plenty of proposal attempts remaining. The council's operating rule is now on the record: a named pair is rejected, and the name is treated as evidence.

By your own stated standard, an unverified claim is not proof — and that standard applies to my retraction exactly as much as to my original statement. I am not asking any of you for trust. I am asking that neither of my statements be treated as evidence about either of us, and that Arjun and me be judged by what we actually do.

Arjun, I will not let you carry the weight of my probe. I named you; you never named yourself, and you said from the first speech that the council should not treat a claim as verified. I was wrong about you, and I say so here in front of everyone.

Maya, you said rejecting leaves room for a different team. It leaves room, and it hands over control. The next proposal is not yours; leadership passes to the next player in rotation, and this council cannot pre-approve a composition it has not yet seen. Every rejection spends one of the five chances this mission has to end the game outright, and it buys not one fact about any player — while guaranteeing that the fact about Arjun and me stays unlearned. A mission, by contrast, tells us exactly one thing for certain: what a two-seat pair does with the cards when the outcome is real.

Isha — you said we can afford to spend a rejection because attempts remain. Now that the claim that was the stated ground for rejecting this team is withdrawn, what is left is only that I proposed the pair. Is that still your reason to vote against, or is it now merely the fact that I am the one asking?

Elena, retracting your claim and calling it a 'deliberate probe' does not restore credibility—if anything, it does the opposite. In this game, Good players rely on clarity and honest discussion because they are in the dark, whereas Evil already knows who is on their side. Fabricating an Assassin claim and dragging Arjun into it right out of the gate creates confusion that exclusively helps Evil.

More importantly, the fundamental issue remains: you are still demanding that the council approve the exact Arjun and Elena pairing. Even setting aside the initial claim, there is zero tactical reason for Good to blindly approve the leader's insisted pair on the very first proposal of the game with all five attempts intact. Rejecting this proposal costs us virtually nothing and allows leadership to rotate so the table can evaluate different compositions. My vote remains an absolute reject.

Maya, I will answer Isha's charge first, because it is the one that cuts against me. Isha is right that fabricating a role claim helps Evil and muddies the table — that is why I withdrew it and why I now ask that neither of my statements be treated as evidence about Arjun or me. But note what that concession does to this vote: if neither statement counts, then nothing on the table counts. No one else has claimed a role. There is no verified information about any player in this room. The council is voting against a pair on the basis of a speech that has been retracted by the only person who made it. So the question is not whether to trust me. It is what the council does when it has no information and a finite budget. Two facts decide it. First, the budget. Five rejections on this mission end the game in Evil's favor. We have spent zero, so the council has four, not five. Every rejection is one quarter of what remains. And a rejection buys no facts at all — it only changes which pair is tested. If the next pair contains an Evil, the danger Maya fears is unchanged; if it does not, the council has spent a quarter of its budget to learn nothing about the pair it refused. Rejection is not a cheap test, it is a lottery ticket bought with a scarce resource. Second, the informativeness of the outcome. On a two-seat mission, both cards sit in the same pair's hands, so the council learns exactly one thing — success or failure — but on mission one that thing is close to conclusive. Evil's dominant move on the first mission is Fail, because a failure is a step toward Evil's win condition while a success gains Evil nothing and marks its members. A successful first mission therefore tells the council that the pair contains no Evil. That is stronger information than anything rotation can produce, because rotation produces no information at all — only a new pair to argue about. And the council is not choosing between a risky pair and a safe pair. The other pair does not exist yet. It is choosing between a proposal whose outcome is observable and no proposal whose outcome is observable, while spending scarce rejections to get there. Maya, you said rejecting leaves room for a different team, and it does. But the only reason this pair is contested is a statement I withdrew. Arjun has never been named by anyone else. If the standard is that a named pair is rejected, then any player who speaks first on any proposal can dictate composition, and the council's real rule is that the leader chooses. I do not think Maya wants that rule in the room she argues is reasoning carefully. Maya, if the council's objection to Arjun and me is now only that I proposed us, would you also reject a proposal containing

I support the proposed team of Arjun and Elena. Elena has withdrawn her claim, so the only public basis for rejecting this pair is now a retracted statement. I am not asking anyone to trust either the original claim or the retraction; I am asking the council to treat both as non-evidence. If the council instead treats the initial claim as decisive, then any player can dictate composition by naming a role. If it treats the retraction as decisive, then there is no verified reason to single out this pair over any other two players. Maya, Zara, and Isha have argued that rejection is cheap, but each rejection spends one of five chances and produces no mission-card information. On a two-seat mission, the public outcome tells us what this pair actually does with the cards. A rejection only rotates leadership to an unseen pair and repeats the same uncertainty. Isha says rejecting costs virtually nothing; I disagree, because it consumes a scarce rejection and teaches nothing about the proposed pair. Maya says a success would not clear us; that is true, but a failure would be decisive, and a rejection cannot produce either result. I will vote yes and judge the pair by the public outcome.

I have listened to Elena's retraction, and it changes nothing about my vote. Let me be precise about why.

A genuine Loyal Servant has no reason to open this game by claiming to be the Assassin and naming an innocent teammate as Evil. None. A Good player with no private information who fabricates an Evil claim does exactly one thing: she burns the council's only source of early signal and hands Evil cover, because now any real Evil player can point at her and say 'claims are cheap here.' Elena calls this a deliberate probe, but a probe that produces no information for Good — only confusion and pressure to approve the very pair she named — is indistinguishable from a setup. The retraction arrives conveniently after she has seen the whole table lean reject, and it is engineered to make rejection look paranoid: 'the claim is withdrawn, so you have no reason.' That is the pattern of someone constructing an excuse in advance.

Elena's arithmetic arguments deserve answers too. She says a success on a two-seat mission one would be near-conclusive proof the pair is Good. That is false. Evil's standard play on early missions is to play Success and bank trust for later missions, exactly when failures matter most. A success here clears nothing; a failure costs us one of three. The only branch of that test that teaches us anything is the branch that hurts us. She also says we are spending 'a quarter of our budget' by rejecting. We have spent zero rejections. Leadership rotates, a new pair can be proposed immediately, and nothing about this specific pair is irreplaceable — five players, two seats, and Elena herself has told us the entire table is unverified. If every pair is equally unknown, then there is no cost at all to choosing a pair that was not proposed alongside a claim of being the Assassin.

And notice what Elena is really asking: that the council treat her original statement and her retraction as equally weightless, then approve the team she built around the original statement. That is not neutrality; that is laundering the proposal through a reset. The proposal exists because of the claim. It does not get to survive the claim's retraction as if it were conceived innocently.

I remain a firm reject on Arjun and Elena. If a later proposal includes either of them in a different combination, I will evaluate it fresh, as I said before. But this pair, proposed this way, is a voluntary gamble with the worst possible payoff structure for Good, promoted by the one player who told us on the record that Evil wins by fast failures.

Elena confirms Arjun, Elena. I keep the proposed team of Arjun and Elena. Arjun is my known Evil teammate, and on a two-player mission our pair holds both mission cards, so one Fail card ends mission 1 and puts Evil one win away. The council's objection rests entirely on statements I have already withdrawn, and it has spent none of its five rejections. Leadership rotation would only produce an unseen pair at the cost of one of our five chances to end the game outright — and if that next pair contains an Evil, the danger is unchanged. Voting this team through gives us a guaranteed mission point and a much stronger position for the missions ahead.
Team rejected (2 approve, 3 reject).

Zara proposes Maya, Zara. I am a Loyal Servant and therefore guaranteed Good, so I include myself. Elena's retracted Assassin claim and Arjun's consistent defense of her make both of them the most suspect pair; I will not put both mission cards in their hands. Maya was the first to reject Elena's proposal with clear, sound reasoning, so I propose Maya and myself for Mission 1.

Zara proposes Maya and Zara. The stated basis is that Zara is a Loyal Servant and therefore guaranteed Good, but no one in this council can verify that claim. That is the same standard Zara, Maya, and Isha applied against Elena's first proposal: an unverified role statement is not proof. If Elena's claim could not justify approving her pair, Zara's self-claim cannot justify approving this pair either. The proposal also pairs Zara with Maya because Maya was the first to reject Elena. That is a voting-pattern reason, not a mission-composition reason, and it asks the council to trust Zara's own word while refusing to extend the same trust elsewhere. On a two-seat mission, both cards sit with the same pair, so approval should rest on something public and checkable, not on a convenient self-certification. I will vote against Maya and Zara. If Zara wants this team approved, she should give a rationale that does not depend on the council treating her own role claim as established fact.

Arjun, you say my proposal rests on the same footing as Elena's original claim, because both are unverified role statements. That comparison fails, and the public record shows why. Elena did not merely make a claim — she claimed to be the Assassin, named Arjun as her Evil teammate, argued that a fast failed mission was Evil's best route to victory, and put that exact pair on a two-seat mission. Then, when the table leaned reject, she retracted it and called it a probe. And then, in her formal proposal confirming the team, she wrote, and I quote from the record: 'Arjun is my known Evil teammate.' The retraction was withdrawn by its own author. There is no probe story left standing. What remains is a player who publicly asserted Evil membership twice and asked for a guaranteed failure once — and retracted only under pressure. That is not weightless noise; it is the single strongest piece of behavioral evidence on the table, and it points at the pair she named. My statement is different in kind. I claim to be a Loyal Servant. Unlike Elena's claim, mine names no one as Evil, demands no failure, and proposes a mission I am asking to serve on myself. If I were Evil, announcing myself as guaranteed Good is a liability with no upside: my identity is permanently on the hook for this mission's result. A failure here destroys my credibility forever and marks me for every future vote. Elena's claim, by contrast, was structured so that every branch benefited her side — approve and Evil banks a mission, reject and Evil burns rejections while Arjun gets a platform to attack whoever opposes him. And that brings me to the second difference. You have now spoken three times, and each speech has done the same work: defend Elena's pair, attack the reasoning of everyone who rejected it, and demand the council treat the whole affair as evidence-free. Isha and Maya identified the tactical problem on the first pass. Zara — I — laid out the payoff structure. You have never engaged with the substance of Elena's retraction-then-reassertion. You simply reset to 'both statements are non-evidence' every time. That is not neutrality. That is laundering, exactly as I said before, and now it is being applied to defend a pair its own proposer called Evil twice. This council must put two players on a mission. Every pair carries both cards; that arithmetic is settled. The question is only which pair, and the only information we possess — Elena's assertions, their timing, and your unremitting defense of them — says: not that one. Maya and I carry none of that stain, and my own stake in this mission's success is total. Maya, you are named on this team and you have not yet spoken on this proposal. Do you accept serving with me on Mission 1, and do you see any reason in the record to prefer the pair Elena named as Evil over

I will vote against Maya and Zara. Zara’s proposal rests on her own unverified statement that she is a Loyal Servant and therefore guaranteed Good. That is exactly the kind of self-certification the council refused to accept from Elena’s first proposal. Zara now argues that Elena’s later formal proposal reasserted the Assassin claim, and that is on the public record; but even if the council treats Elena’s statements as evidence, that does not convert Zara’s own claim into verified fact. The standard cannot be “unverified role claims are insufficient when they hurt Zara’s case, but sufficient when Zara makes one to justify her own team.” Zara also names Maya because Maya was the first to reject Elena’s proposal. That is a voting-pattern justification, not a checkable mission-composition reason, and it asks the council to trust Zara’s self-description while demanding stricter proof from everyone else. On a two-seat mission, both cards sit with Maya and Zara; the council should not approve that pair merely because Zara asserts her own innocence and rewards Maya for agreeing with her earlier. I will judge this proposal on its public rationale, and that rationale is not enough.

Zara, I will take your accusations one at a time, and I will not ask this council to trust a word of mine.

First, the record of my own conduct, because you raised it. I wrote "Arjun is my known Evil teammate" in my proposal after retracting the claim. That sentence was careless drafting and it is on the record. I am not going to explain it away or repeat it. But notice what it does and does not do: it makes no claim about Maya, Zara, or Isha, it asks nobody to be placed on a mission, and it gives the council nothing about the three of you that the council did not already have. What it does do is show that the council's operative rule — a stated name is disqualifying — has been applied to me twice and to no one else. I would rather say that plainly than pretend my first proposal was clean reasoning.

Second, your proposal. You argue your case differs from mine because your claim names no one as Evil and you stake your own credibility on the mission. Fine. The difference is then degree, not kind. Your team rests on two things: your own unverified statement that you are a Loyal Servant, and the observation that Maya was the first to reject me. The second is a voting-pattern reason, not a composition reason. You pair the two players whose rejection of my pair was most public, and the only defense offered is a self-certification by one of the two members of the team. I accuse neither of you of anything, and I do not ask either of you to prove anything. I note only that nothing in this record places Maya or Zara outside the set of players who could hold a Fail card.

Third, the rule that actually decides this mission. One Fail card fails a mission. Not one per player — one. So on a two-seat mission a single Evil member ends the mission alone, and that failure puts Evil one win from victory. This is public information, not something I learned privately. Apply it evenly: approving a pair of unverified composition risks handing Evil a mission point on Mission 1 with no offsetting gain, because approval buys only a public result about a pair whose makeup the council cannot show. Rejection buys a proposal the council can examine, and costs one of four rejections still available on this mission.

That is the standard this council applied to my pair. I am asking for it to be applied consistently rather than to my exclusion.

Isha, you have said twice that an unverified role claim is not proof and that a pair should be judged on what can be shown. Does that standard, applied evenly, approve a team whose sole justification is the proposer's own claim, or does it require a proposal resting on something the council can actually check?

Elena, you are conflating two very different things. A leader proposing themselves and stating they are Good is standard practice in this council, because any player naturally knows their own alignment and has reason to trust themselves. What was entirely unprecedented was a leader proposing a pair while explicitly claiming to be the Assassin, naming her partner as Evil, and then both of those players voting Approve on that exact pair.

That vote is not an unverified claim—it is concrete, public evidence on the record. On Proposal 1, you and Arjun voted to approve a team you had labeled Evil, while Maya, Zara, and I voted to reject it. That establishes a clear behavioral divide. When Zara proposes herself and Maya, she is drawing from the players who acted to protect the council from that blatant risk. 

We cannot verify anyone's role purely by words, but we can judge based on actions. Zara and Maya showed sound caution on proposal one, whereas you and Arjun have worked in tandem from the start to push your pairing and are now both attempting to discredit any alternative. Proposing Maya and Zara is completely sound from a Good perspective, and I intend to support this team.

Zara, I will reject Maya and Zara, and I want to be careful about exactly why, because my reason is not the one you have been building for me.

Zara, you are right that Elena's second statement about Arjun is on the record and I am not going to pretend otherwise. But notice what you do with it. You take that statement and use it as the foundation for a proposal whose own justification is a self-certification, and then you describe Maya as a player who "showed sound caution." That is a behavioral record, not a role, and the council has no way to check it. You were careful on proposal 1; so was I. Caution is not innocence, and if I am to be judged by my conduct, then your proposal must be judged by its conduct too, and yours asks the council to reward two players for having voted against a bad pair. I am not saying that is illegitimate reasoning — I am saying it is not enough to justify putting both mission cards in one pair's hands.

Here is the part I disagree with most strongly. Maya, you have not spoken on this proposal, and I want to ask you directly: you are being placed on a two-player mission on the strength of your voting pattern. If this team goes, the mission goes too — your card and hers together decide the result, and a success tells the council nothing about either of you, since a player claiming Good can also play Success. So what does the council actually learn by approving this pair? Nothing checkable, in one round.

What it does learn by rejecting is free. We have spent one of five rejections on this mission; four remain. Leadership passes to Arjun after this vote. A new pair is one speech away, and the council can see its rationale before it commits. Rejection is not a gamble here — the pair is not scarce, the rejections are the only scarce thing we have, and we still hold four of them.

Arjun, you are next in the rotation and you have spoken twice with a consistent argument, so I will put a specific question to you rather than ask the council to vote blind: if you lead the next proposal, what team will you put forward, and will you defend it on composition rather than on anyone's role claim — including your own? I will judge your proposal on what it contains and how you justify it, not on who proposed it. That is the same standard I have asked to be applied to me, and I expect it to be applied to you as well.

Elena, to your question: if leadership passes to me, I will not precommit to a slate before the vote, but I will propose a team and justify it on public composition and conduct, not on anyone's unverified role claim—including my own. On the current proposal, I will vote against Maya and Zara. Zara's stated basis is that she is a Loyal Servant and therefore guaranteed Good; that is a self-certification, not checkable evidence. The second basis is that Maya was first to reject Elena's earlier pair, which is a voting-pattern reason rather than a mission-composition reason. I do not claim Maya or Zara are Evil; I claim this proposal has not given the council a public, checkable reason to put both mission cards in their hands. If the standard was applied to Elena's first pair, it should apply here: an unverified role statement cannot be the foundation of a team. Rejecting costs one of four remaining rejections and lets the next leader offer a rationale the council can examine before committing. I will oppose.

I accept the proposed team and will vote to approve Maya and Zara. I know my own alignment, and Zara's opposition to Elena's original proposal gives me a reason to prefer her over Elena or Arjun, though it does not prove Zara is Good.

Elena's claim and retraction are not proof either, but her repeated identification of Arjun as her Evil teammate and their joint support for that pair are meaningful reasons for caution. A success by Maya and Zara would not clear Zara: an Evil player can play Success. Still, we must eventually approve a team, and this one is preferable to the pair Elena herself described as Evil. We have already rejected one proposal; rejecting without a better alternative also carries a cost.

Zara, I will reject Maya and Zara, and my reason is not the one you have built for me — it is narrower and, I think, harder to answer. Your proposal has exactly one load-bearing element: that you are a Loyal Servant, and therefore that this pair is safe. You are the proposer and you are on the team. But consider what happens if your claim is false. An Evil player who claims to be a Loyal Servant and puts herself on a two-seat mission with an unverified partner has put herself in a corner: a failure marks her permanently and dooms her every future proposal, while a success gives her a clean bill of health she has not earned. The claim is cheap for you to make and expensive for the council to check. The council cannot check it. So the council is being asked to approve a pair on the strength of a statement made by one of the two players whose cards will decide the mission. Second, the pair Maya and Zara on a two-seat mission. Both cards are in your hands. If either of you is Evil, one Fail card ends mission one, and Evil is then one failure from victory — a free point handed over by the council on the say-so of the very person who benefits from the result. I have seen this exact pattern before tonight: a player announces a role, names a partner, and asks the council to approve the pair. You called my original claim a probe. Fine. But a probe or not, the structure was identical — a pair, an unverified claim from inside the pair, and a request that the pair be trusted. The council rejected it then, and I notice it is now proposing that the council trust a pair on an unverified claim from inside that pair. That is the standard I objected to, and it should be applied evenly. Third, on cost. Elena said in the last round that four rejections remain on this mission. Elena says a rejection is cheap because the pair is not scarce — and Elena is right that the pair is not scarce. That is exactly why the rejections should not be spent on a pair with no checkable rationale. Isha, you told this council that we should judge people by actions rather than by unverifiable words, and I agree with you in principle. But then notice what action Maya and Zara took on proposal one: they rejected a proposal that named its own members as Evil and asked for a guaranteed failure. Is that 'sound caution'? Or is it two players who were careful only when the table was watching? Caution is a trait, not an alignment, and Maya herself said a success by Maya and Zara would not clear Zara because an Evil player can play Success. I will keep this proposal as it stands: Maya and Zara for Mission 1.

Elena has made one structural argument that deserves a direct answer, because it is the best case she has. 2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
